titre: Natalie Kalmus, the woman shipped with every Technicolor camera
accroche: From 1934 to 1949, every Technicolor film is credited to the same color director, whom the studios could not turn down.
contenu_vulgarise:
In March 1939, in the middle of production on *Gone with the Wind*, producer David O. Selznick complains in an internal memo that Technicolor's experts have been “putting all sorts of obstacles in the way of real beauty.” In 1944, on *Meet Me in St. Louis*, director Vincente Minnelli recalls that he “couldn't do anything right in Mrs. Kalmus's eyes.” The first produces the film, the second directs it. Yet on the color of a dress or a wall, neither has the last word.

## A Camera No Studio Owns

The three-strip process that Technicolor perfected in 1932 rests on a singular camera. Behind the lens, a beam-splitter cube divides the light: one third passes through a green filter and exposes a first strip of film, while the rest passes through a magenta filter and goes to two other strips, one that records only blue, the other only red. Three black-and-white films are thus shot at once. At the lab, each one becomes a dyed matrix, cyan, magenta or yellow, and the three dyes are transferred one after the other onto the print the public sees.

Technicolor does not sell this camera. It rents it, along with its operators and a supervisor responsible for checking that sets, costumes and makeup stay within what the process can render. This supervisor is very often Natalie Kalmus. She heads the company's art department and appears in the credits of every Technicolor film produced from 1934 to 1949, under the title of color director, which she prefers to that of consultant. In 1939, according to the New York Times, she earns $65,000 a year.

Her authority comes neither from an invention nor from a patent. It comes from a lease: to shoot in three-strip, you have to rent the camera, and the camera comes with her. Kalmus does not always refuse. On *Doctor X*, in 1932, Fay Wray prefers a dark blue dress to the recommended turquoise; Kalmus gives in, knowing that this blue will turn green on screen.

## What This Shifts

It is tempting to picture the color of classic Hollywood as the product of chemistry, or of the taste of a few great cinematographers. For fifteen years, it also passes through the eye of a single person, imposed by a rental contract. And this person is not what the credits suggest. Natalie and Herbert Kalmus, cofounder of Technicolor, divorced in secret as early as 1922. She kept the name, the job and the signature. In 1948, she sues her former husband for alimony and names Technicolor among the defendants, claiming half the assets of the company whose taste she had represented on every set. She does not win her case, and her name leaves the credits after 1949.

repere.texte: In 1939, according to the New York Times, Natalie Kalmus earns $65,000 a year as a Technicolor executive. She is then credited on all of the company's films, even though her divorce from cofounder Herbert Kalmus dates back, in secret, to 1922.
repere.source: Wikipedia (in English), “Natalie Kalmus,” after the New York Times, 1939

carte.punch: For fifteen years, Hollywood's color passed through the eye of a single woman.
carte.idee: Technicolor did not sell its three-strip camera: it rented it, along with a color supervisor. From 1934 to 1949, Natalie Kalmus is credited on all of the company's films and stands up to Selznick as well as Minnelli. Her power came not from a patent, but from a lease.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full history of the company's processes, from the first two-color experiments to the abandonment of the three-strip camera.

quiz.question: Where did Natalie Kalmus get the power to impose her color choices on Hollywood's greatest directors?
choix: She had herself invented the three-strip process in 1932
Technicolor rented out its camera with her, and never sold it
A federal law required a color controller on sets
She personally held the patent on the camera
quiz.explication: Kalmus neither invented the process, which was perfected by the company's engineers, nor held its patent, and no law required a controller. Her authority came from the lease: Technicolor did not sell its camera, it rented it along with its technicians and its color supervisor.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On Doctor X, in 1932, what happens when Fay Wray prefers a dark blue dress to the recommended turquoise?
choix: Kalmus gives in, knowing that this blue will turn green on screen
Kalmus refuses and has the scene reshot with the turquoise dress
The director decides in Kalmus's favor
The dark blue dress is repainted in the studio to correct the shade
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that, on Doctor X, Kalmus gives in to Fay Wray's choice while knowing that the dark blue will turn green on screen.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What title does Natalie Kalmus prefer to that of “consultant”?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that she appears in the credits under the title of color director, which she prefers to that of consultant.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Natalie Kalmus obtain in 1948, when she sues her former husband and names Technicolor among the defendants?
choix: Her own department within the studio
Nothing: she does not win her case
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that in 1948 she claims half of Technicolor's assets but does not win her case, and that her name leaves the credits after 1949.
